label: Denavit-Hartenberg Parameters
notes: This appendix spans printed pages 585 through 596 and asks one guiding question: how do four numbers per joint encode an entire serial chain, and when is the product-of-exponentials picture clearer? We treat D-H as a frame-assignment discipline, keeping the geometry inspectable rather than memorizing a formula list.

label: Serial Chains and Link Frames
notes: A serial manipulator is a chain of rigid links joined by single-degree-of-freedom joints. Forward kinematics needs a frame on every link. D-H supplies a minimal, reproducible recipe for placing those frames so that only four parameters relate each neighbor, instead of the six a general rigid transform would demand.

label: The Common Normal Rule
notes: The heart of the convention is geometric. Point each frame's z-axis along its joint axis, then choose the x-axis along the common normal between consecutive joint axes. This single shared line fixes the origin and orientation enough that the relative pose collapses from six free numbers down to four.

label: The Four DH Parameters
notes: Each link row carries four numbers: link length a measured along the common normal, link twist alpha rotating one z-axis onto the next, link offset d sliding along the joint axis, and joint angle theta. Revolute joints vary theta; prismatic joints vary d. The other two stay fixed by the mechanism.

label: The Link Transform
notes: The relative pose between neighboring link frames factors as a fixed sequence of two screw motions: a screw about x carrying twist alpha and length a, then a screw about z carrying angle theta and offset d. Because SE(3) is noncommutative this order is rigid, and swapping factors describes a different frame entirely.

label: Transform as a Matrix
notes: Writing each elementary rotation and translation as a homogeneous matrix and multiplying gives the closed form of the link transform. The rotation block mixes theta and alpha through sines and cosines, while the translation column records a along x and d along z, expressed in the previous frame's coordinates.

label: Forward Kinematics by Composition
notes: Forward kinematics is then pure matrix bookkeeping: chain the per-link transforms in order from base to tip. Each factor depends on exactly one joint variable, so the end-effector pose is an ordered product, and the chain rule on this product later yields the manipulator Jacobian cleanly.

label: A Two-Link Worked Example
notes: For a planar two-link arm both twists vanish and both offsets are zero, so each row reduces to length a and angle theta. Multiplying the two transforms reproduces the familiar tip position with summed angles, a check the notebook computes numerically to confirm endpoint agreement with a screw-axis model.

label: DH versus Product of Exponentials
notes: D-H compresses a chain into a compact four-column table, ideal for hand work and consistency checks. Product-of-exponentials keeps each joint screw explicit in one shared frame, exposing axes directly. When conventions and home pose agree the two give identical kinematics; disagreements are convention mismatches, not deep failures.

label: Ambiguities and Singular Cases
notes: The convention has sharp edges worth naming. When neighboring axes intersect the common normal has zero length, and when they are parallel a whole family of normals exists, so frame placement must be stated explicitly. Sign conventions can also migrate between parameters, which is why a table without a diagram is dangerous.

label: Takeaways
notes: D-H stays valuable for compact serial-chain tables and quick hand kinematics, while product-of-exponentials often reveals geometric screw axes more directly. The reliable habit is to name the representation and its invariant together, always pairing a D-H table with a frame diagram so another reader can reproduce the same chain unambiguously.
